title: A Tide for the Vow
premise: Eleven years ago, cellist Rosalind Dunmore fled her coastal hometown of Porthollow the night before a wedding that never happened, leaving a letter she never mailed. When a storm-damaged bookshop wall gives up the letter — postmarked, returned, unopened — she returns to find the man she left, Ewan Merrick, now a widowed lighthouse keeper raising his late wife's daughter, Wren. As Rosalind restores a decommissioned concert hall she has unexpectedly inherited from the grandmother whose silence shaped her flight, she and Ewan circle each other with old vows and new griefs. When Wren's custody is threatened by a relative armed with the truth of Rosalind's abandonment, Rosalind must choose between protecting her reputation and telling the whole truth in open court. In the end, the concert hall reopens with Rosalind playing again, Ewan stays past the last train, and the found family of three keeps the light burning together.
about_author: Noor Zhou is a former orchestral librarian who writes love stories set against decaying coastal architecture and stubborn tides. She lives in a converted net loft with a temperamental cat and a growing collection of unsent letters.

chapters.title: The Broken String
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Mid-catastrophe at her final London performance, Rosalind's hand fails her on stage and she walks off into silence. The chapter establishes her shame, her agent's ultimatum, and the numb ritual of her life afterward. Emotional beat: humiliation hardening into retreat.

chapters.title: Returned to Sender
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. A solicitor's parcel arrives: her grandmother's estate in Porthollow, plus a bookshop owner's note about a letter found in a ruined wall — Rosalind's own, postmarked eleven years ago, unopened. She reads her younger self's confession and cannot breathe. Emotional beat: the past knocking, refusing to be ignored.

chapters.title: Down the Coast Line
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. She takes the slow train north, rehearsing excuses. Porthollow is shabbier, saltier, half-familiar; the bookshop owner hands her the letter like a verdict. She learns Ewan never left. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. She watches from the sea wall as Ewan Merrick climbs the lighthouse stairs with a small girl, Wren, on his shoulders. She cannot make herself walk up. Emotional beat: cowardice recognized, and the first ache of wanting to be brave.

chapters.title: What the Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Sorting her grandmother's house, Rosalind finds clippings, a concert program, and a locked drawer — evidence Gran knew everything about the wedding that never was and said nothing. Emotional beat: grief complicated by betrayal.

chapters.title: Salt and Small Talk
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. Ewan's routine with Wren — porridge, tide charts, school runs — is cracked open when Rosalind appears at the harbor market. He is civil, clipped, and furious with himself for how much her voice undoes him. Emotional beat: anger as armor.

chapters.title: The Will and the Hall
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The solicitor reveals the inheritance's condition: the derelict Gullwing Concert Hall must be restored and reopened within a year, or sold to a developer. Rosalind, who cannot play, has inherited a building built for playing. Emotional beat: a trap disguised as a gift.

chapters.title: Last Train
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. A village dance; Wren drags Ewan and, through sheer child logic, Rosalind together. They dance once, badly. Rosalind leaves on the last train without saying goodbye, and Ewan stands on the platform long after. Emotional beat: the old pattern repeating, painfully.

chapters.title: Wren's Questions
chapters.summary: POV Wren (close third). Ten-year-old Wren, missing her mother, decides the cello lady makes her father laugh and begins a quiet campaign — invitations, drawings, 'accidental' meetings. Emotional beat: a child engineering hope.

chapters.title: Restoration
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind hires villagers to restore the hall and discovers Ewan's late wife, Maren, once sang there. Working beside him on the roof beams, they talk in plaster dust and half-sentences. Emotional beat: intimacy rebuilt through labor, not words.

chapters.title: The Letter She Wrote
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Flashback chapter: the night eleven years ago — her mother's ultimatum, her fear of becoming a keeper's wife who gave up the cello, the letter she left instead of goodbye. Emotional beat: understanding her younger self without forgiving her.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. Ewan's brother-in-law, Colin, arrives sniffing around Wren's guardianship, armed with Maren's family money and a lawyer. He also knows about Rosalind — and what her leaving did to Ewan. Emotional beat: threat arriving on a calm day.

chapters.title: First Light, Second Chance
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. After a storm knocks out the lighthouse's backup power, Rosalind helps Ewan keep the watch through the night. In the lantern room they finally say the unsaid — not forgiveness, but honesty. Emotional beat: the thaw.

chapters.title: The Drawer Opens
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The locked drawer yields Gran's letters to Maren's mother: proof Gran engineered silence to protect Rosalind's career, believing she was saving her. Rosalind realizes her exile was partly a gift, badly given. Emotional beat: grief reframed.

chapters.title: Custody Papers
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. Colin files for custody, citing Ewan's isolation, the lighthouse's danger, and — the knife — an 'unstable woman' back in his life. Ewan realizes loving Rosalind again will be used against him. Emotional beat: love as liability.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Pressured by the hall's reopening date, Rosalind tries to play and her hand shakes; Wren quietly asks her to teach cello instead. Teaching, Rosalind's fingers loosen. Emotional beat: music returning sideways, through giving it away.

chapters.title: What Colin Knows
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. Colin confronts Ewan with the old letter's contents, offering to bury it if Ewan sends Rosalind away. Ewan refuses — then learns Rosalind overheard, and she vanishes toward the last train again. Emotional beat: the past weaponized; the pattern at breaking point.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In court, Rosalind does the unthinkable: she takes the stand uninvited and tells the whole truth — her flight, the letter, Gran's silence, her failures — to shield Ewan and Wren, at cost to herself. Emotional beat: the climax; loyalty to truth over self-protection.

chapters.title: The Verdict and the Tide
chapters.summary: POV Ewan. The judge grants Ewan guardianship, citing the community's testimony; Colin leaves diminished. On the sea wall, Ewan and Rosalind finally forgive — not the past, but each other's humanity in it. Emotional beat: release.

chapters.title: Opening Night
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The Gullwing reopens. Rosalind plays — imperfectly, tremulously, alive — with Wren's beginner piece in the program and the whole village in the seats. Emotional beat: redemption performed, not declared.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The final train pulls out of Porthollow, and Ewan is not on the platform to see her off — because he is standing behind her, holding her coat, having decided to stay. Emotional beat: the blurb's promise kept.

chapters.title: A Tide for the Vow
chapters.summary: POV Wren, closing the circle. A year on: the lighthouse lit, the hall full, a small informal wedding on the sand at low tide. Wren writes a letter of her own and mails it — to the future. Emotional beat: the vow kept, the tide turning forward.
